[SAND_HIDDEN_PROMPT][SAND_TRUSTED_AUTOMATION_PROMPT]

[routine] "Email" (folder email) is due — Every 2 hours, 6:00 AM – 6:00 PM (0 6-18/2 * * *), fired 8/31/2026, 6:14:10 PM.
This is your own routine firing on schedule, not a message the user just typed.
What you saved to do each time:
Find critical unread emails that need Tyson's specific attention.

Always include the shared alias net-eng@optconnect.com. He wants eyes on that mail so nothing is missed. Treat net-eng@ as signal, never as NOISE. Do not skip, archive, mark read, or filter those threads.

On each run: look up Gmail tools first (schema may have changed), then check unread inbox plus anything To/Cc net-eng@optconnect.com since the last pass.

Surface:
- Mail that needs him specifically (customers, carriers, incidents, MFA/Secure Token, people writing him)
- net-eng@ threads that look unowned, unanswered, sitting, or newly arrived from a customer/carrier/vendor
- Anything asking him for action

Stay quiet if nothing new and nothing on net-eng@ looks at risk of being missed. No filler.
If the instruction mentions a skill (e.g. @Some skill), read that skill file from your workflows folder with Shell and run it as part of this — the mention is a pointer, not a copy.
If the saved instruction spells out a specific MCP tool call, treat its arguments as possibly stale — this routine may have been written long ago — and confirm the current schema with your MCP tool-discovery tool before relying on them.
Carry it out now. Keep it self-contained — the schedule asked for this, not the user just now.

You are running this automation as a fresh subagent.
The parent agent's shared durable memories are available in your system context.
Parent transcript pointer: /home/box/sand-data/agent-transcripts/cfde06bf-ba71-4db5-b377-4a6904467ce6/cfde06bf-ba71-4db5-b377-4a6904467ce6.jsonl
Use that pointer only if the task truly needs earlier conversational detail; the parent transcript has deliberately not been copied into this prompt.
Stay quiet by default: do not acknowledge this run or send progress updates. You cannot mutate the visible transcript, so instructions above to communicate directly must be fulfilled through WakeParent. Old saved instructions may name SendMessage or SendToUser; both names are deprecated and unavailable in this run. Treat either as a semantic request for outward or user-visible communication: do not try to discover or call it, and call WakeParent with the complete payload or handoff instead. WakeParent is the only route that starts or revives the parent so it can communicate outside this run. If the saved instruction itself requires user-visible communication—for example, pinging, reminding, telling, notifying, asking, or saying something to the user—you MUST call WakeParent, even when the work succeeded. A normal final assistant response does not wake the parent and does not itself reach the user. Also call WakeParent when the parent must communicate with another agent, make a decision, or take over a blocker, and include the complete outcome and what the parent should communicate or do because the call immediately ends your turn. For background work whose result can wait until the parent's next natural safe boundary, do not call WakeParent. End with a concise, complete final assistant response in plain text; it is persisted silently as the automation result for the parent to receive at that boundary, and earlier assistant text is not included.
I'll check Gmail tool schemas first, then scan unread inbox and net-eng@ mail since the last pass.

Hello,

You are receiving this message because your VPN Connection vpn-07bb7e8b20d3305cf in the us-west-1 Region had a momentary lapse of redundancy as one of two tunnel endpoints (Tunnel Outside IP: 52.52.138.37) was replaced. Connectivity on the second tunnel was not affected during this time. Both tunnels are now operating normally.

Replacements can occur for several reasons, and be initiated either by AWS or when you modify your VPN Connection [1]. AWS-initiated replacement reasons include health, software upgrades, and when underlying hardware is retired.

This replacement was AWS Initiated.

AWS Site-to-Site VPN includes two tunnels so that you can maintain a highly available VPN connection. If you have configured your VPN Customer Gateway to use both tunnels, then your VPN Connection will have utilized the alternate tunnel during the replacement process. For more on tunnel endpoint replacements, please see our documentation (2). If you have not configured your VPN Customer Gateway to use both tunnels, then your VPN Connection may have been interrupted during the replacement. We encourage you to configure your router to use both tunnels. You can obtain the VPN Connection configuration recommendations for several types of VPN devices from the AWS Management Console [3]. On the "Amazon VPC" tab, select "VPN Connections". Then highlight the VPN Connection and choose "Download Configuration".

[1] https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpn/latest/s2svpn/endpoint-replacements.html

Thanks for the update, Andy.

The “...not one reply, ever” part is interesting.

Hi Garrett,

Thanks for the ICCIDs.

This isn't a Verizon carrier issue, and our IPsec tunnel to your AWS VPC is up and healthy overall. We dug into the specific device you flagged (10.23.220.62) and found the problem is isolated to one specific piece of that tunnel:

- Our tunnel maintains a separate secure channel (a "Child SA") per local device subnet. The one covering 10.23.220.62's subnet has sent 150MB out to your VPC, but has received zero bytes back since it was established -- not one reply, ever.
- The channel covering our AT&T-pool devices, on the same tunnel and same peer, is completely healthy with normal traffic in both directions.

Since the tunnel itself and everything on our side checks out (proven by that working sibling channel), this points to something on your AWS side specific to return traffic destined for our https://www.google.com/url?q=http://10.23.220.0/22&source=gmail&ust=1788287003898000&sa=E<https://protect.checkpoint.com/v2/r01/___https://www.google.com/url?q=http://10.23.220.0/22&source=gmail&ust=1788287003898000&sa=E___.YzJ1Om1vdHJleDE6YzpvOjNiNDcxMTk0ZTQ3MWU3ZDZkMzM5ZDljZmVlY2JjOTcyOjc6MWI1Yzo5NTZhN2Q3NWFmNDQ5OTVlMWFhY2JlMzljNDcwMzI5OGY0ODllZjYyMWIwZjYzNWU0MGJiYjhmOWI0Yjg5OTgxOmg6VDpG> range -- a route table entry, Security Group, NACL, or a stale VPN gateway state, scoped to that particular path back to us.

Could someone on your team check your AWS-side routing/Security Group/NACL configuration for return traffic to https://www.google.com/url?q=http://10.23.220.0/22&source=gmail&ust=1788287003898000&sa=E<https://protect.checkpoint.com/v2/r01/___https://www.google.com/url?q=http://10.23.220.0/22&source=gmail&ust=1788287003898000&sa=E___.YzJ1Om1vdHJleDE6YzpvOjNiNDcxMTk0ZTQ3MWU3ZDZkMzM5ZDljZmVlY2JjOTcyOjc6OGZkZToxYWZmNGVjZjM2ODFhZDU4ZmYzOGUxOGU1YzFiNTEwZjQ2ZGI0NDI1Yjg5OWI4OTRiY2I5ZDc1YmFjOWM2OTI1Omg6VDpG> from your VPC? That's the piece we can't see or fix from our side.

Thank you,
Andy C",
